title: Nice to meet you
goal: Greet people, give your name, ask how someone is, say where you're from — and see why the Persian word for "is" sticks to the end of a word.
bekal: say hello and goodbye in formal and casual situations
give your name, origin, and nationality in full sentences
use the six endings that do the job of "am / is / are"

dialogs.title: گفتگو — در لابیِ هتل
dialogs.intro: First day in Tehran. Two people are waiting for the elevator in the lobby of a small hotel.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: من هم خوبم. اسمِ من بودی است.
lines.baca: man ham khubam. esm-e man Budi ast.
lines.id: I'm fine too. My name is Budi.
lines.literal: I also good-I. name-of I Budi is.

lines.speaker: رضا:
lines.id: Nice to meet you. My name is Reza.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: من اهلِ اندونزی هستم. شما ایرانی هستید؟
lines.baca: man ahl-e Andonezi hastam. shomâ irâni hastid?
lines.id: I'm from Indonesia. Are you Iranian?
lines.literal: I native-of Indonesia am-I. you Iran-i are-you?

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: شیراز خیلی زیبا است. من عاشقِ شعرِ حافظم.
lines.baca: Shirâz kheyli zibâ ast. man âshegh-e she'r-e Hâfezam.
lines.id: Shiraz is very beautiful. I'm a huge fan of Hafez's poetry.
lines.literal: Shiraz very beautiful is. I lover-of poetry-of Hafez-I.

lines.speaker: رضا:
lines.text: چه خوب! پس شما مهمانِ ما هستید.
lines.baca: che khub! pas shomâ mehmân-e mâ hastid.
lines.id: How nice! Then you're our guest.
lines.literal: what good! so you guest-of we are-you.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.id: That's very kind of you. Goodbye.

notes: ***Khubam*** **= خوب + ـَم, and that is where "am" hides.** Unlike Arabic, Persian does have a verb "to be" — but it doesn't stand on its own; it sticks to the end of the word before it as a little tail. خوب ("good") + ـَم = خوبم ("I'm fine"). English puts "am" in front as a separate word; Persian tacks it onto the end.

**Three ways to say thanks: متشکرم، ممنون، مرسی — take your pick.** متشکرم (*moteshakkeram*) is the most formal and the longest. ممنون (*mamnun*) is the everyday one. مرسی (*mersi*) comes from French and sounds perfectly natural to Iranian ears — people in Tehran say it dozens of times a day. The reply to "thank you": خواهش می‌کنم (*khâhesh mikonam*).

**The prefix خوش makes happy words.** خوشبختم literally means "good-fortuned I am" (خوش "good" + بخت "fortune"). The same prefix gives خوشحال (*khoshhâl*, glad), خوشمزه (*khoshmaze*, tasty), خوشگل (*khoshgel*, pretty), and خوش آمدید (*khosh âmadid*, welcome — literally "well came you"). Whenever you see خوش at the start of a word, the meaning is almost certainly pleasant.

**Always use شما with people you've just met.** شما is really the plural ("you all"), but it is used to one person as a mark of respect — like French *vous*. تو (*to*) is only for family, close friends, and children. Using تو with a stranger sounds rude; using شما with a close friend just sounds stiff. When in doubt, choose شما. The details are in unit 5.

**In اهلِ کجا, the little mark ـِ is not decoration.** The -e sound linking the two words is called the **ezafe**, and it is the backbone of Persian. This book prints the mark so you don't misread; Iranian books and newspapers never print it at all. All of unit 3 is devoted to it.

***Khodâ hâfez*** **literally means "God (is your) keeper".** It is the most common goodbye, fine with anyone. More formal: به امیدِ دیدار ("till we meet again"). Most casual: فعلاً (*fe'lan*, "for now") — roughly "see ya". In Tehran speech خدا حافظ is often shortened to خدافظ (*khodâfez*), much like "goodbye" comes from "God be with you".

grammars.title: The "is" that sticks to the end of the word
body: This is the most important lesson of unit 1, and the good news is you can master it today. Persian expresses "am / is / are" with six short endings attached to the last word of the sentence. The ending shows **who** is being talked about, so the pronoun in front can often be dropped.
after: There is also a **long form** that stands alone: هستم، هستی، هست، هستیم، هستید، هستند. It means exactly the same. The long form is used for emphasis or when the word before ends in a vowel: من ایرانی هستم sounds clearer than من ایرانی‌ام, although both are correct.

⚠️ If the word before ends in a vowel, the short ending is joined with ء or ی: ایرانی → ایرانی‌ام, خسته → خسته‌ام (*khaste-am*, "I'm tired"). If that feels complicated, just use the long form — it is always correct and never misread.
The negative is one word for each person: **نیستم، نیستی، نیست، نیستیم، نیستید، نیستند**. من ایرانی نیستم = "I'm not Iranian".

grammars.title: Six personal pronouns — and no gender
body: Here is one of Persian's great gifts to learners, so enjoy it now: **او means both "he" and "she".** There is no هو and هي as in Arabic, no *il* and *elle* as in French. One word covers both — English has to choose; Persian never does.
after: The pronoun او is only for **people**. For things and animals, use آن (*ân*, "that") or این (*in*, "this").
Because the verb ending already tells you who, the pronoun can be dropped: خوبم alone means "I'm fine", no من needed. Use the pronoun for emphasis — **من** خوبم = "*I'm* fine (as for me)".

blocks.text: Notice the pattern بخیر (*bekheyr*, "with goodness") added to صبح، عصر، شب. The same pattern appears in سفر بخیر (*safar bekheyr*, "have a good trip") and روز بخیر (*ruz bekheyr*, "good day").
These aren't grammar to study — they're emergency tools. Memorize them whole now; understand how they're built later.

The word ببخشید works both ways: it apologizes **and** gets someone's attention in the street ("excuse me"). For a heartfelt apology, Iranians say معذرت می‌خواهم (*ma'zerat mikhâham*) or شرمنده (*sharmande*, literally "I'm ashamed").

blocks.title: A Persian phrase with no equivalent
items: ***Khaste nabâshid*** (**خسته نباشید**) — literally "may you not be tired". You say it to anyone who is working or has just finished: the taxi driver as you get out, the shopkeeper after you pay, the teacher when class ends. English has nothing like it, and saying it instantly makes you sound like someone who really knows Persian.
The reply: سلامت باشید (*salâmat bâshid*, "may you be healthy") or simply ممنون.

blocks.title: One sentence that changes your trip
items: "I'm learning Persian. Please speak Persian." — من فارسی یاد می‌گیرم. لطفاً فارسی صحبت کنید. (*man fârsi yâd migiram. lotfan fârsi sohbat konid.*)

The typical problem when learning Persian in Iran isn't unfriendly people — it's the opposite: Iranians are wonderfully hospitable, and the moment they hear your accent many switch to English, thinking they're helping. The sentence above stops that politely, and almost everyone will gladly stay in Persian — usually while praising you lavishly.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: سلام، حالِ شما چطور است؟ — من خوبم، متشکرم. — اسمِ من بودی است. — شما اهلِ کجا هستید؟ — من اهلِ اندونزی هستم.
خوش آمدید — خسته نباشید — خواهش می‌کنم — نمی‌فهمم — ببخشید
من اهلِ اندونزی هستم. — اسمِ من رضا است. — حالِ شما چطور است؟ — از آشنایی با شما خوشحالم. — من ایرانی نیستم.
